The Arab Kings.

and he was a disciple of Abu'l-Barakat, the Jewish physician of Baghdad.
This man moved from Baghdad to Mosul,
and from there to Azerbaijan,
and from here to Khilat,
and entered the service of the Shah-Arman,
and acquired much property in this service of his.
And during one of the king's illnesses, when he took his urine sample to examine it as usual,
one of the servants said to him:
"Why do you not taste it,
O physician?" And the physician did not answer him at the time,
but after he went outside, he called him and said to him privately:
"Did someone else instruct you to tell me to taste the urine,
namely, the king himself or someone of his household,
or did you say the word on your own?" And the servant replied:
"No,
but I heard them saying
that taste also has diagnostic value in urine,
just as do color, odor, and consistency (or consistencies)."
And the physician said:
"That is so,
but not in every disease.
And know that you have done me a great injury with this remark of yours,
because when the king heard this, he would suppose that I do not discharge in his service all the duties I am obligated to fulfill."
And from then on, that physician grew uneasy in his mind,
and was no longer comfortable there.
And he also gave a sum of money to that servant,
and persuaded him not to speak to him in this manner again.
And when after some time he asked to be dismissed from service,
he obtained permission and departed from Khilat,
and came and settled in Mosul,
and remained there until he died.
At the end of his days he became blind;
and many used to come to him and learn the art of medicine thoroughly.
Now he lived for ninety-five years,
and wrote a marvelous book on medicine,
in four volumes,
and called it *Mukhtar* (The Choice Book);
and behold, many read and study it today.
And in this same year,
which was the year six hundred and ten of the Arabs [1213-1214 AD],
Genghis Khan desired to go in person to Persia.

all the amirs there, with their armies, entered his service:
